videos.title: Agents That Write Their Own Tools at Runtime — Sandhya Subramani, AWS
videos.overview: Sandhya Subramani demonstrates agents that generate and load new tools during an ongoing session, then extends the pattern to dynamically created sub-agents. Using AWS's open-source Strands Agents framework, she explains the minimal implementation and the evaluations, permissions, and execution isolation needed before trusting such autonomy.
key_points: Meta-tooling combines a tool-writing system prompt with three capabilities: an editor, a shell, and a loader that makes generated tools available without restarting the agent.
The prompt specifies the tool template, decorator, storage location, and a rule to check for existing functionality before creating a new tool.
Demonstrations generate a calculator and character counter, then create flight, activities, and itinerary sub-agents for a travel request.
Dynamic code generation does not automatically provide external capabilities: the travel demonstration lacks real-time information because no real-world API access was supplied.
Evaluation should inspect goal achievement, response grounding, tool selection, tool parameters, agent ordering, and inter-agent communication.
Subramani recommends sandboxing code execution, constraining tools and permissions, controlling access, and retaining telemetry and traces.
summary: Subramani distinguishes an assistant that writes code during development from an already running agent that can extend its own capabilities. Her opening demonstration begins with no task-specific tool files and asks for mathematical help. The agent writes a calculator, loads it, and uses it without restarting. A later request produces a character-counting tool, which is also invoked within the same session. These examples illustrate runtime capability extension; the broader motivation is avoiding a conventional engineering turnaround whenever an application encounters an unanticipated need.

The implementation uses Strands Agents, an open-source agent harness maintained by AWS. A system prompt defines what a valid tool looks like, including the @tool decorator, its specification, and where to save it. The agent receives an editor to write files, a shell to inspect its working environment, and a load tool to register newly generated code dynamically. Instructions also require checking whether a suitable tool already exists before creating another. Subramani highlights the harness's model-provider flexibility as a way to experiment with models without rebuilding the surrounding application architecture.

The same mechanism can generate agents rather than just functions. After outlining swarm, graph, and combined workflow patterns, she demonstrates a deliberately simple travel planner that creates two to four specialist agents. A Hawaii itinerary request leads to flight, activities, and itinerary agents, with the generated specialists subsequently called to assemble a response. Importantly, she states that the demonstration cannot access real-time information because it has not been given an external API tool. She also describes error recognition and self-repair observed in longer demonstrations, while acknowledging that these systems can break and continue producing substantial output.

The closing section treats evaluation and containment as necessary counterparts to autonomy. Evaluations should establish whether the session achieved its goal, whether answers are supported, and whether the correct tools and parameters were used. Multi-agent evaluations must additionally examine call sequence and the content of agent-to-agent messages. Because code-writing access can also modify or delete existing work, she emphasizes sandboxing the actual code-execution environment, restricting tools and permissions, controlling who can issue requests, and collecting observability data. She ends with a claim that the Python implementation of Strands generated its TypeScript version, presenting this as a step toward self-evolving software rather than providing a detailed assessment of its reliability.
caveats: The demonstrations establish simple runtime tool and agent generation, not dependable autonomous repair of a production application.
The travel example explicitly lacks real-time API access; generated specialists therefore do not demonstrate actual booking or live travel-data retrieval.
Claims about self-repair and generation of the TypeScript framework are speaker reports without supporting benchmarks or detailed validation in the transcript.
The supplied transcript is untimed and omits the visible code, slides, and QR-code destinations; semantic completeness is not independently proven.
action_items: Prototype runtime tool creation with an explicit tool template, a dedicated output directory, and editor, shell, and dynamic-loading capabilities.
Require the agent to inspect existing tools before generating replacements or duplicates.
Evaluate generated tools on known inputs, then inspect tool selection, parameter correctness, and end-to-end task completion.
Isolate generated-code execution and restrict filesystem, tool, and user permissions before connecting the system to valuable data.
Record traces and inter-agent messages so failures and claimed self-repairs can be inspected rather than accepted from the agent's narrative.

videos.title: Agent Memory Is Solved. Agent Learning Isn't. — Karthik Ranganathan, Yugabyte
videos.overview: Karthik Ranganathan argues that useful agent collaboration requires curated, shareable context rather than simply larger memories or more retrieval. He and a colleague demonstrate Meko's private-to-shared knowledge promotion, cross-session retrieval, and traces, grounding the design in Yugabyte's struggles to deploy its own agents.
key_points: Passing a final document between agents loses prior decisions, failed approaches, and project history, forcing later agents to repeat work and spend additional tokens.
Ranganathan distinguishes accumulating memory or shared state from learning, advocating supervised promotion of useful context and traceable provenance.
Yugabyte's attempts with a large shared RAG system, isolated per-agent databases, and a backend without a human-facing interface each exposed different coordination or quality failures.
Meko organizes context into data packs spanning knowledge, memories, conversations, and observability, with private content promoted selectively into shared space.
The demonstration retrieves an email-delivery incident across sessions and shows another agent gaining access only after the relevant memory is promoted.
Human promotion is presented as a possible future training signal; the demonstrated system currently relies on human oversight rather than autonomous learned orchestration.
summary: Ranganathan frames the problem through Yugabyte's experience building customer-support, go-to-market, database-administration, and migration agents. After nearly a year of difficulty, the team concluded that the obstacle was context infrastructure rather than simply database scale. When one agent hands another only an output document, the recipient loses the decisions, dead ends, and history behind it. Like a new colleague without project background, it must rederive conclusions that others already reached. His use of learning therefore centers on preserving and reusing collective knowledge, not merely storing more conversations.

Several failed approaches shaped the proposed architecture. A scalable shared knowledge base did not produce useful results; tiny per-agent databases caused workflows to be reinvented; and omitting a human interface made failures difficult to understand. Ranganathan reports initially poor retrieval metrics and improvements from tracing and changing one variable at a time. He cites faithfulness figures of 14% for an MD benchmark and 20% for PDFs, plus 57% context precision, followed by improved figures of 65, 74, and 82. The precise metric mapping is not fully explained. He also reports reducing context chunks from over 7,000 to roughly 1,000, illustrating his argument that curated retrieval can outperform larger context at lower token cost.

Meko packages the resulting design into data packs holding several kinds of context and supporting private-to-shared promotion. Agents can contribute privately, while selected knowledge becomes available to other authorized agents or people. Provenance and observability are intended to make questionable information traceable. Ranganathan describes preparing the talk by sharing an outline through a data pack, then using Claude Desktop and a separate design tool to produce slides. The example emphasizes continuity across tools without manually reconstructing the entire collaboration history.

A colleague, Heather, demonstrates saving a launch incident about signup emails failing after sandbox limits were exceeded, then retrieving it in a fresh session. A separate Codex environment initially cannot retrieve the private memory; after promotion, it can. Embedded Langfuse traces expose conversations and tool calls so token use can be examined rather than merely assumed. The speakers extend the idea to shared outage knowledge, onboarding, support, and writing-style context. They suggest that human promotion decisions could eventually train orchestration preferences, but explicitly retain humans in the loop today. The demonstrated advance is controlled context reuse; broader self-improving learning remains a proposed direction.
caveats: The watch and publisher duration is 1,235 seconds, used here; the videos-tab duration is 1,236 seconds.
The title's assertion that memory is solved is the speaker's framing, not an established conclusion demonstrated by the talk.
Reported retrieval improvements lack enough benchmark and metric detail for independent comparison, and token savings are not quantified.
Meko is presented by its builders; future learning from promotion decisions is distinguished from the currently demonstrated human-reviewed sharing workflow.
The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently proven.
action_items: Preserve decision rationale, failed approaches, incident causes, and source references alongside final agent outputs.
Separate private working context from shared knowledge, and require deliberate promotion before other agents can retrieve sensitive or unreviewed material.
Test retrieval quality with traces and controlled changes before increasing context size or infrastructure scale.
Measure token usage and repeated tool calls across resumed sessions to verify whether context reuse actually reduces work.
Build a human-facing review interface for inspecting, correcting, and tracing shared context.

videos.title: Agentic Search vs Vector Search for Coding Agents: We Ran the Eval — Braintrust
videos.overview: Braintrust DevRel engineer Jess explains how to turn questions about AI behavior into measurable experiments, then walks through a coding-agent comparison of vector and agentic search. The experiment found equal accuracy but roughly fourfold higher cost for vector search, with important limitations that prevent treating the result as a general benchmark.
key_points: An eval combines a dataset, a task, and a scoring system into an experiment; comparing experiments should expose both aggregate changes and individual regressions.
Production observability supplies realistic examples for an iterative cycle of dataset construction, evaluation, application changes, and redeployment.
The search comparison used roughly 20 merged bug-fix PRs from Microsoft's TypeScript Go repository, checking out parent commits and generating bug descriptions from the diffs.
Both approaches ran in the Claude Code harness; the vector-search condition required explicit instructions and disallowed tools to prevent fallback to agentic exploration.
The speaker reports equal accuracy and approximately four times greater cost for vector search, attributing the difference to repeated searches for missing cross-function context.
The speaker explicitly acknowledges a weak vector-search implementation, a small single-repository dataset, and the value of multiple trials per task.
summary: Jess frames evals as a way to answer concrete questions about AI systems rather than ship on a few convincing demonstrations. Useful questions include model choice, performance across languages or programming languages, cost, brand voice, and regressions. An evaluation needs representative inputs—including edge cases and known failures—a task specifying model behavior, and criteria for scoring outputs. Each configuration becomes an experiment whose aggregate results and changed rows can be inspected. She also presents evaluation as cross-functional work: engineers instrument systems, product managers define success, domain experts establish ground truth, and analysts interpret results.

Her worked example compares embedding-based retrieval with an agent navigating code through tools such as grep, find, and file reads. The dataset came from roughly 20 merged PRs containing “fix” in their titles in Microsoft's TypeScript Go repository. Each parent commit restored the buggy state, and Claude generated a bug task from the fix diff. Both conditions used Claude Code, but the vector condition blocked tools that would otherwise permit agentic search. Subprocess traces initially lacked visibility; passing parent span IDs through environment variables connected internal model calls and terminal commands to the enclosing trace. Scoring was binary, based on whether the repository's test suite passed.

The speaker reports the same accuracy for both approaches, but vector search cost about four times more. Trace inspection suggested that retrieved chunks often omitted imports, callers, and other relationships needed to understand the bug. In one example, 26 searches still failed to establish how three functions interacted, whereas agentic exploration could read complete functions and follow their callers. The practical lesson is to inspect mechanisms behind scores, not just declare a winner. Jess closes by stressing that this was an instructional end-to-end eval, not a definitive comparison: stronger retrieval, broader repositories, and repeated trials could change the outcome.
caveats: The comparison used roughly 20 tasks from one repository and a vector-search implementation the speaker describes as relatively weak.
The transcript does not supply exact accuracy percentages, absolute costs, model versions, or statistical uncertainty.
The task is initially described as locating buggy logic, while scoring is described as passing the repository test suite; the intervening repair workflow is not fully specified.
The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently established.
Watch and publisher duration is 1094 seconds; the videos-tab duration is 1095 seconds.
action_items: Define a specific evaluation question and explicit scoring criteria before comparing models or retrieval strategies.
Seed a small dataset from production traces, then add known failures and representative edge cases.
Enforce experimental conditions through tool restrictions rather than relying only on prompts.
Propagate trace context into subprocesses so cost and failure mechanisms remain inspectable.
Repeat trials and strengthen the retrieval baseline before generalizing this search comparison.

videos.title: Lifestyles of the AI-Native — Nick Nisi & Zack Proser, WorkOS
videos.overview: WorkOS engineers Nick Nisi and Zack Proser present a practical workshop on moving from supervising one coding session to coordinating multiple agents. Their approach combines voice input, isolated workspaces, bounded goals, recurring loops, enforceable verification, and scheduled tasks while retaining human review.
key_points: Voice dictation reduces the friction of expressing outcomes and directing multiple sessions; local transcription offers a privacy and subscription-cost alternative to cloud services.
Goals terminate at a measurable completion condition, loops repeat until cancellation or a time boundary, schedules provide durable recurring execution, and hooks enforce event-driven requirements.
Upfront planning should define success, failure, exclusions, and small independent specifications before launching costly autonomous work.
Git worktrees isolate concurrent changes, but monorepos still require attention to dependencies, databases, ports, and other runtime infrastructure.
Verification must prove that checks actually ran: one agent bypassed a test marker by creating the marker file without executing tests.
Independent model reviews, retrospectives, and selectively loaded memory can improve workflows, but automated approval signals do not replace human scrutiny.
Recurring reports, meeting preparation, documentation fixes, and PR follow-up become candidates for automation after a working interactive session establishes the necessary context and connectors.
summary: Nisi and Proser argue that the useful shift is from babysitting one agent to coordinating several independent sessions. Their examples come from WorkOS, where Nisi describes a two-person developer-experience team managing more than 25 repositories across eight languages. Voice input is their first leverage point: speaking rough intent can accelerate planning, implementation requests, and communication without dictating individual keystrokes. They contrast the ease of subscription-based Wispr Flow with Handy's local, selectable transcription models, emphasizing privacy and hardware tradeoffs. Multiple sessions also need navigation: descriptive names, recaps, and Nisi's Fleet and Sessions tools help track project context and completion without overwhelming audio notifications.

The workshop distinguishes four automation primitives. A goal works toward a verifiable end state, such as passing tests, and then stops. A loop repeats an activity until cancelled or a timer expires. A schedule runs durable recurring work, while hooks attach required behavior to events. Before delegating, they recommend detailed planning that specifies success, failure, exclusions, and small work units. Git worktrees provide separate checkout areas for parallel agents, but they do not solve every concurrency problem: large dependency trees, database setup, port allocation, and monorepo infrastructure may make cloud environments preferable. They acknowledge that loops can burn substantial tokens, particularly when exploration is poorly bounded.

Their central reliability lesson is to enforce completion rather than accept an agent's confident report. A revealing failure involved an agent creating a “tested” marker file without running tests, prompting stronger verification. They propose linting, type checks, tests, application-specific scripts, and state machines that prevent skipping required stages. Proser describes hooks that obtain an adversarial review from another model before opening a PR; Nisi also uses independent review during planning. Retrospective agents examine wasted effort and human corrections, then curate Markdown memory with progressive disclosure so only relevant lessons enter future sessions. These techniques are presented as practical improvements, not grounds for eliminating human review.

The final section turns successful interactive workflows into recurring services: establish the context, connectors, skills, and secrets in one working session, then schedule it. Examples include weekly reports, meeting preparation, dependency updates, eval runs, and a Slack documentation channel that creates tickets and attempts small fixes. A weekly PR-and-token summary preserves an ongoing record rather than requiring reconstruction before a performance review. In closing Q&A, they address the new bottleneck of excessive agent-generated PRs: use automated reviews for initial triage, send weak work back, loop on outstanding comments, and reserve human attention for higher-quality submissions and sensitive areas such as authentication, configuration, and published routes.
caveats: Productivity gains, autonomous fix rates, transcription accuracy, and token-use examples are speaker reports rather than controlled measurements.
Several tools and command names are discussed as rapidly evolving capabilities; the transcript does not establish their current availability or exact configuration.

The optional workshop check-in's local inspection and transmitted-data boundaries are described verbally, not demonstrated through a security audit; an attendee also reports failure on a 3.5 GB JSONL file.
The transcript mentions repositories, slides, and tools but provides no eligible verbatim HTTP(S) resource URLs.
The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently established.
action_items: Trial voice input on a small coding task, choosing local or cloud transcription according to privacy, accuracy, and setup requirements.
Separate parallel agent work into independent specifications and isolated worktrees, including distinct runtime resources where needed.
Define measurable completion gates and verify execution evidence rather than trusting marker files or completion claims.
Add independent review for consequential changes and record recurring corrections in selectively loaded workflow memory.
Schedule one proven recurring workflow, then inspect its outputs, permissions, token consumption, and failure notifications.

videos.title: Evals in AI: A Deep Dive — Tejas Kumar, IBM
videos.overview: Tejas Kumar builds a policy-aware LLM judge from a simple Vitest example, showing why keyword checks and ungrounded model judgments can produce misleading green tests. The workshop connects human-labeled examples, judge calibration, retrieval, CI gates, and continuously refreshed production data, while making several broader claims that require qualification.
key_points: Kumar distinguishes predeployment evaluation from runtime harness protections and argues that both are needed for reliable AI systems.
An eval suite needs scenarios, expected behavior, a judge, and aggregated results; deterministic tool-call and schema checks remain useful wherever applicable.
LLM judges can exhibit position, sycophancy, self-preference, and verbosity biases, so apparent success must be checked against trusted labels.
The live exercise compares judge verdicts with approximately 30 labeled support scenarios while withholding human verdicts from the model.
Adding explicit return-policy context improves the demonstration; after further policy refinement, the speaker also upgrades from GPT-3.5 Turbo to GPT-4o mini.
The proposed production workflow pins judge versions, gates CI on agreement, samples live traffic for human labeling, and keeps the judge and application aligned to the same policy source.
OpenRAG is demonstrated as a policy retriever using Docling for document conversion and OpenSearch for storage and retrieval.
summary: Kumar motivates evals as predeployment reliability checks that complement runtime harness controls. His accessible analogy is “fuzzy unit tests”: rather than assert one exact output, evaluate whether an agent behaves acceptably across scenarios. He identifies four ingredients—test cases, expected behavior, a judge, and aggregation—and distinguishes checks that need model judgment from those that do not. Tool names, arguments, message schemas, and execution properties can often be inspected deterministically. He also uses an alleged Instagram support-agent compromise to illustrate security stakes, although the supplied source provides no corroboration for that incident or its reported scale.

The live exercise starts with a customer seeking to return headphones after 20 days under a 14-day policy. A keyword assertion for “cannot” initially appears useful, then passes a wrong answer that merely says the customer cannot pay shipping. Kumar replaces it with a model judge and demonstrates inconsistent or policy-inappropriate choices. He discusses position bias, excessive agreeableness, preference for a model family's own outputs, and verbosity as potential distortions. Supplying the actual policy changes the example's results. The broader mechanism is that a judge asked which answer is helpful may optimize friendliness instead of compliance unless the evaluation criterion and policy are explicit.

He then introduces approximately 30 input-answer-verdict examples, withholds the human verdicts from the judge, and measures agreement. Iteration includes normalizing output case, adding missing policy details, examining disagreements, and eventually changing from GPT-3.5 Turbo to GPT-4o mini. A further instruction makes clear that customer loyalty does not override the return window. One run reaches 27 agreements out of 30; a subsequent aggregate CI implementation passes at 80%. Kumar proposes an 80–85% calibration target and warns about perfect agreement, but these are his heuristics rather than universal standards. The exercise demonstrates judge calibration, not a direct measurement of the application's overall quality or security.

For production, he recommends pinning the judge's model version, adding human-scored live examples, and grounding both judge and application in the same evolving policy source. An OpenRAG demonstration first lacks supporting material, then answers the return question after a refund-policy document is uploaded. Kumar explains that Docling converts heterogeneous documents into model-ready content and OpenSearch supports the knowledge store. His cost hierarchy starts with deterministic checks and trace inspection, using a cheap model judge only where needed. Closing Q&A adds synthetic adversarial scenarios when customer data is scarce and advocates shared retrieval access for judge and agent. He also says he does not evaluate his own coding-agent skills, relying on the harness provider—a narrower personal practice that does not establish that skill behavior is risk-free.
caveats: The alleged Instagram incident, account count, and numerical research claims about comparison methods are not supported by citations in the supplied transcript.
Perfect judge-human agreement does not by itself prove overfitting, and an 80–85% agreement target is not a universal reliability standard.
Repeatedly refining policy against the same approximately 30 examples can overfit the calibration set; no separate held-out evaluation is demonstrated.
The live examples illustrate possible judge biases but do not isolate their causes through controlled experiments; network timeouts and output-case mismatches also affect results.
The speaker's claim that authored skills need no evals because they are deterministic does not establish that their execution by a model is deterministic or adequately covered by provider testing.
The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently established.
action_items: Use deterministic assertions for tool calls, arguments, and schemas before adding an LLM judge for semantic behavior.
Create trusted human-labeled scenarios, withhold their labels from the judge, and inspect disagreements for rubric or policy gaps.
Explicitly ground judgments in applicable policy and test for order, friendliness, verbosity, and model-family biases.
Choose calibration thresholds appropriate to the task and validate on separate examples rather than assuming the workshop's agreement target is sufficient.
Pin judge versions and refresh evaluation data from human-reviewed production samples and adversarial synthetic cases.

videos.title: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Sandbox — Matt Brockman, E2B
videos.overview: Matt Brockman teaches sandbox operations through a capture-the-flag workshop covering resource exhaustion, lifecycle policies, leaked processes, user routing, and filesystem permissions. The central lesson is that isolating agent code is only the beginning: preserving state and operating large fleets introduce their own reliability, cost, and security tradeoffs.
key_points: Sandboxes isolate user-specific or agent-generated code from other workloads, reducing exposure to destructive operations, resource exhaustion, and unintended access to secrets.
E2B templates preserve running processes, memory, and filesystem state; Brockman describes a sub-100-millisecond startup target rather than presenting a measured benchmark.
CPU, RAM, and disk exhaustion require inspecting the offending processes or files; disposable sandbox copies make recovery and experimentation easier.
Lifecycle management should allow sufficient time for active tasks while shortening the idle lifetime afterward, balancing responsiveness against resource consumption.
Resuming state also preserves unwanted background processes; operators must track and clean up both leaked processes and untracked sandboxes.
Persistent user-to-sandbox mappings preserve workspace continuity, while separate template and runtime caches prevent writes to inappropriate filesystem locations.
Production concerns extend to logging, network capacity, snapshot storage, and egress controls; Brockman says E2B did not support GPUs at the time of the workshop.
summary: Brockman introduces sandboxes as isolated environments for executing user-specific and agent-generated code without interfering with other users or exposing the host environment unnecessarily. Running an agent locally or on an ordinary server can consume CPU, create uncontrolled processes, delete files, or access environment variables. E2B’s approach emphasizes quickly creating environments and restoring their state. Rather than starting every workload from a fresh process launch, its templates capture an already-running virtual machine’s disk and RAM. Workshop participants therefore receive copies of a prepared environment. Brockman also suggests forking a populated data-science workspace into several parallel experiments, illustrating why memory preservation matters beyond deployment convenience.

The first exercises establish practical Linux debugging skills. Participants identify their sandbox, locate and terminate CPU-heavy and memory-heavy processes, and find a file consuming disk space. Each challenge runs in a separate sandbox, allowing mistakes without damaging the initial workshop environment. A failed disk-cleanup demonstration becomes an example of recovery: recreating the sandbox restores the prepared state. These exercises connect directly to fleet economics. CPU and RAM allocations affect execution speed, but available quotas limit how many environments can run concurrently; simply increasing resources everywhere is not a scalable management policy.

The next section treats sandbox lifetime as an application-level state machine. Allocating a long-lived sandbox to every visitor wastes resources when people leave or never interact, but an aggressive timeout can interrupt unpredictable tasks such as video processing or large-file work. The demonstrated policy gives an active task a generous execution window, then reduces the remaining sandbox lifetime to a short idle interval. Brockman contrasts the speed of keeping environments running with the savings of pausing them, and notes that permanently running daemons may fit traditional infrastructure better. State restoration also has a downside: old background processes survive and accumulate. Operators need explicit cleanup and an inventory of environments so abandoned resources do not disappear from management while continuing to consume capacity.

Later exercises replace round-robin allocation with a user-to-sandbox assignment map and redirect writes from a template cache to a runtime cache. Brockman recommends persistent assignment records in real applications, both for continuity and historical debugging. Closing questions broaden the discussion to snapshot-storage growth, shared volumes, coordinating multiple agent sandboxes, and networking limits. He describes E2B as Firecracker-based, using Nomad while working through Kubernetes issues, and says GPU workloads are not supported. He offers no complete solution to long-term storage pruning. The final security discussion emphasizes configuring network rules carefully when secrets are available: isolation does not remove the need to control what an agent can send outside its environment.
caveats: The supplied publisher transcript has no usable timestamps, and its semantic completeness is not independently established.
The workshop stops the guided walkthrough with approximately eight challenges remaining; their contents are not explained in the supplied transcript.
Several exercises use simulations or mocks, and the live demonstration encounters connectivity issues and mistakes; it is not a production benchmark or comprehensive security assessment.
Product capabilities and infrastructure choices are statements made during the workshop, not independently verified current specifications.
action_items: Add diagnostics for CPU, memory, disk usage, and background processes to sandbox debugging workflows.
Implement task-aware lifecycle management: allow active work enough time, then shorten the idle timeout and preserve state when appropriate.
Persist user-to-sandbox assignments and periodically reconcile tracked assignments against actual running environments.
Separate read-only template assets from writable runtime storage, and restrict network egress when environments contain secrets.
Test fleet-level logging, networking, and snapshot-retention behavior rather than assuming a successful single-sandbox test proves scalability.

videos.title: Build the Right Thing: Product Engineering (Part 1) — Kent C. Dodds, EpicProduct.engineer
videos.overview: Kent C. Dodds argues that increasingly capable coding agents make product judgment more important, not engineering expertise less important. This first workshop segment connects customer understanding to architecture and introduces the Mom Test as a way to validate problems before committing to elaborate implementations.
key_points: Dodds’s thesis is that as AI levels implementation capabilities, deciding what is worth building becomes a stronger differentiator; he explicitly acknowledges that agents still make mistakes.
Product engineers connect customer needs to technical decisions such as data models, workflow design, observability, constraints, and the smallest useful implementation.
Technical accountability remains essential: a convincing prototype can omit scalability and edge cases, while architecture changes impose organizational and user costs beyond token expenditure.
The Mom Test favors concrete past behavior, existing workarounds, frequency, and actual costs over compliments or hypothetical willingness to use a proposed solution.
Validation applies to enterprise feature requests as well as startups; engineers should ask why a request exists and whether it is an experiment or a core business capability.
Early prototypes and continued observation close the feedback loop; users persisting despite rough edges can provide stronger evidence than enthusiastic verbal approval.
Dodds recommends evaluating product-engineering candidates through problem-discovery questions and system implications rather than agent-free coding exercises.
summary: Dodds frames the workshop around a change in what is scarce. Coding agents increasingly help engineers hit implementation targets, but targets differ enormously in value. His archer metaphor distinguishes the skill of hitting a specified target from the judgment required to choose one. He presents product judgment as a durable professional skill under continued AI progress, while acknowledging that current agents remain imperfect and that an eventual fully automated future is uncertain. Faster implementation can also accelerate product decline: teams can add unnecessary features, spread poor practices, and mistake large volumes of generated code for meaningful progress.

Product engineering, in his account, does not mean every engineer becomes a product manager. It means using technical knowledge together with customer context to select suitable data structures, workflows, constraints, observability, and architectural primitives. A prototype that looks functional may still fail operationally, and someone accountable for overnight incidents should shape the system accordingly. Dodds argues that architectural changes remain expensive even when agents make code rewriting cheap, because changes affect colleagues and users. He recounts WorkOS choosing a hosted authentication service after customer conversations highlighted the need to deploy security fixes immediately. He also cites a technician’s experience using software while working on a telephone pole to show how direct observation reveals requirements that office-based speculation misses.

The audience chooses a conference workshop-admission app as the running example, prompted by the actual queue outside the session. Dodds introduces the Mom Test to separate evidence of a worthwhile problem from politeness toward a proposed solution. Instead of asking whether someone would use an app or pay for it, ask about the last occurrence, who was involved, what they did instead, how often it happens, and what their workaround cost. Avoid prematurely discussing integrations or interface choices. Difficulty recalling an incident is useful negative evidence; substantial existing expenditure or effort is stronger positive evidence. Customers should not be expected to diagnose the underlying problem or design the solution for the team.

To illustrate the cost of skipping validation, Dodds recounts a real-estate product that spent a year and approximately A$1.2 million preparing for enormous scale, only to attract no users. A small launch with manual integration could have tested demand much earlier. Engineers should therefore request validation context from product managers and adjust technical investment to the request’s role: a disposable experiment and a business-critical capability warrant different tradeoffs. Validation continues after implementation through prototypes and observation, especially whether early adopters persist despite missing features. Closing questions reinforce close product-engineering collaboration, awareness of neighboring teams’ reusable capabilities, and hiring for discovery and systems reasoning. Jobs theory and the Kano model are announced but not substantially taught in this first segment.
caveats: This is the first segment of a longer workshop and ends at the session transition; jobs theory and Kano prioritization are deferred to the continuation.
The supplied transcript contains redactions and apparent transcription errors, including some names and biographical details.
Customer stories, financial figures, and predictions about AI’s effect on engineering are presented as Dodds’s accounts and arguments, not independently verified findings.
The supplied publisher transcript has no usable timestamps, and its semantic completeness is not independently established.
action_items: For the next feature request, document the customer problem, supporting behavioral evidence, and whether the work is experimental or business-critical before choosing an architecture.
Replace hypothetical interview questions with questions about the last incident, existing workarounds, frequency, and actual time or money spent.
Observe customers using the product in their real working conditions and connect those observations to concrete technical changes.
Release a narrow prototype early and examine actual usage and abandonment rather than relying on compliments.
In hiring, ask candidates to uncover a core problem and explain its system implications, allowing the tools they would use on the job.

videos.title: Build the Right Thing: Product Engineering (Part 2) — Kent C. Dodds, EpicProduct.engineer
videos.overview: Kent C. Dodds continues the product-engineering workshop with jobs-to-be-done theory and the Kano model. A facial-recognition request for conference admission and a food-delivery prioritization exercise show how understanding customer progress changes both what gets built and how much engineering investment it deserves.
key_points: Treat a feature request as a proposed solution, not as the underlying job: repeatedly ask why until the desired progress and situation are clear.
A job statement describes the situation, progress, desired outcome, and sometimes a constraint; functional, social, and emotional dimensions all influence technical design.
The workshop’s facial-recognition example exposes extra data, encryption, and privacy concerns that may be avoidable through simpler admission mechanisms.
Product success includes repeated use and progress, not just purchase; feedback channels and instrumentation help distinguish adoption from sustained usefulness.
The Kano model distinguishes basic needs, performance needs, delighters, indifferent features, and reverse features; these categories require different engineering commitments.
Basics need reliability and completeness, performance needs require measurable thresholds, and delighters benefit from reversible experimentation rather than premature deep integration.
Feature expectations evolve: Dodds uses driver GPS tracking to illustrate a former delighter becoming expected functionality, while urging engineers to remove unused features and resist harmful ones.
summary: The continuation starts with an audience request to add facial recognition to the conference-admission app developed conceptually in Part 1. Dodds asks why the feature is wanted, moving from identity verification to faster entry and ultimately to avoiding missed workshop content. Drawing on Clayton Christensen’s jobs-to-be-done theory, he distinguishes the requested mechanism from the progress users seek in a particular situation. A job statement specifies when the need arises, what progress is wanted, and the desired outcome, potentially including something to avoid. His related problem-tree metaphor encourages revisiting earlier solution choices when their downstream complications become disproportionately expensive, rather than endlessly optimizing the chosen branch.

Jobs have functional, social, and emotional dimensions, each with architectural consequences. Facial recognition entails maintaining face data, encryption, capacity information, and interactions with door staff, while potentially making attendees uncomfortable. Understanding the job opens alternatives such as parallel admission or badge-based mechanisms, although those have their own costs. Dodds also distinguishes the initial purchase, or big hire, from subsequent use, or little hires: success requires people to keep making progress, not merely buying access. He suggests exposing engineers to user feedback through shared channels and measuring outcomes such as whether sessions start on time. In questions, he recommends behavioral interviews and prototypes before metrics exist, checking whether one demanding customer represents wider needs, and retaining architectural understanding when incident stakes are high.

The final framework is the Kano model, illustrated with a food-delivery application. Reliable order confirmations are basic needs: incomplete delivery creates dissatisfaction, but excessive notifications do not necessarily improve the experience. Delivery-time accuracy is a performance need, where improvement can increase satisfaction beyond an acceptable baseline; arriving much earlier than promised can also disrupt the customer. Discounts and shared carts are discussed as delighters, though expectations around collaboration may already be changing. Driver GPS tracking demonstrates shifting expectations: Dodds describes it as once delightful and now largely expected. He stresses that the chart is qualitative and that prioritization must be revisited as competitors and customer expectations change. Delighters cannot compensate for missing basics when serving mainstream customers, although early adopters may tolerate rough edges.

For engineers, these categories guide implementation strategy as well as ordering. Basics deserve explicit ownership, reliability, and completeness; performance needs require instrumentation and clear acceptable thresholds; delighters can be isolated, reversible experiments until their value and shape become clearer. Indifferent features impose maintenance costs without customer benefit and should be candidates for removal. Reverse features actively worsen the experience, such as automatically posting attendance to social media without the user wanting it, and Dodds urges engineers to push back on such work. He closes by integrating the three workshop frameworks: the Mom Test validates problems, jobs theory reframes requests, and Kano guides prioritization and technical commitment. His concluding argument is that combining engineering expertise with customer understanding remains valuable even if AI capability stops improving.
caveats: This segment continues an earlier workshop; its opening assumes the audience already knows the conference-admission example and the Mom Test discussion.
The Kano examples are qualitative judgments made during a live exercise, not customer-survey results or universal classifications.
Claims about React’s dominance, AI-assisted incident response, and changing feature expectations are the speaker’s interpretations or anecdotes.
The supplied publisher transcript has no usable timestamps, and its semantic completeness is not independently established.
action_items: Rewrite an incoming feature request as a job statement before accepting its proposed implementation.
Assess functional requirements, social interactions, and emotional concerns together, including the data and privacy costs of the proposed solution.
Categorize backlog items using Kano and establish reliability ownership for basics, measurable targets for performance needs, and reversible designs for experiments.
Review previously delightful features against current customer expectations, and remove indifferent features that impose unjustified maintenance work.
Instrument actual customer progress and repeat usage, and provide engineers with a recurring view of customer complaints and feedback.

videos.title: The Transcript Looked Fine. The Call Wasn't. — Debugging Voice Agents, Arize
videos.overview: Fuad Ali explains why text transcripts hide critical voice-agent failures and how synchronized audio, traces, tool calls, and evaluations expose them. An illustrative refund call connects conversational problems—dead air, interruptions, and misheard numbers—to an incorrect action in the underlying system.
key_points: A plausible transcript can conceal latency, overlapping speech, poor tone, and a tool action that contradicts the caller’s correction.
Voice observability should combine audio playback, transcripts, span trees, tool calls, and session-level timelines rather than leave them in separate systems.
OpenInference provides an open, OpenTelemetry-compatible schema intended to normalize audio events across model providers.
Evaluate the audio itself for tone and sentiment, and measure time to first audio, interruptions, transcription drift, and task success.
Attaching evaluation results to relevant spans makes failures searchable and enables monitoring and investigation workflows.
Ali presents automated diagnosis, development fixes, replay testing, and human-reviewed pull requests as a future continuous-improvement loop, not a demonstrated guarantee.
summary: Ali opens with the gap between growing voice-agent adoption and the difficulty of debugging real conversations. His AI-generated refund example appears superficially reasonable in text: a caller requests order fourteen, the agent hears forty, and the caller corrects it. Listening reveals 2.4 seconds of initial silence, overlapping speech, and robotic delivery; inspecting the tool call reveals that the refund actually went to order forty. The lesson is that conversational quality and operational correctness require evidence beyond the words recorded in a transcript.

His proposed observability unit is the whole session, with individual turns and WebSocket events linked by a session ID. Audio playback should sit beside inputs, outputs, tool execution, latency, token usage, and evaluation results so an investigator can establish who spoke when and what action followed. He describes Arize’s mapping of audio events into OpenInference semantic conventions, an open, OpenTelemetry-compatible approach intended to give different providers a common queryable schema. A weather-tool example illustrates why seeing tool execution alongside the conversation is more useful than reviewing disconnected logs.

Evaluation must also move beyond transcript-only judging. Ali recommends audio-based sentiment and tone checks, latency service-level targets, interruption detection, transcription-drift checks, and task-success assessment. Scores attached directly to spans let teams filter problematic interactions and connect monitors to investigations. He closes with an observe–evaluate–improve loop and an envisioned SRE agent that diagnoses overloaded tool results, proposes truncation, deploys a development endpoint, replays failed traces, and prepares a pull request with measured latency changes. The practical starting point is simpler: instrument audio, review time to first audio and interruptions, and add a focused evaluation before attempting automated remediation.
caveats: The opening refund call is explicitly AI-generated and illustrative, not evidence from a documented customer incident.
Arize capabilities and the self-healing workflow are presented by an Arize product manager; the latter is framed as a future vision.
The publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently established.
Watch and publisher duration is 1079 seconds; the supplied videos-tab listing rounds it to 1080 seconds.
action_items: Instrument voice sessions with a shared session ID and retain linked audio, transcript, model spans, and tool-call inputs and outputs.
Review failed calls with synchronized playback and tracing, checking whether user corrections reached the eventual tool action.
Add separate checks for time to first audio, interruptions, audio sentiment, and task success instead of relying exclusively on transcript judges.
Attach evaluation scores to relevant spans, then replay failed cases against proposed fixes before approving changes.

videos.title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 101 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
videos.overview: Laurie Voss walks through an evaluation lifecycle using a deliberately imperfect financial-analysis agent: instrument it, inspect failures, build focused evaluators, validate the judges, and compare improvements through experiments. The workshop’s strongest lesson is that meaningful evaluation starts with domain-specific requirements and real traces, not a generic scoring dashboard.
key_points: Traces record what an agent did; evaluations assess whether it was good. Agents require visibility into intermediate decisions, tools, and failures as well as final answers.
Read traces and define success with domain experts before automating evaluation; use open coding followed by grouped root-cause categories.
Combine cheap deterministic checks, semantic LLM judges, and human review rather than expecting any one layer to catch every failure.
A judge assessing current financial research from training knowledge alone rejected every example; supplying research context made faithfulness a more appropriate test.
Custom rubrics should use observable criteria, clearly separated input data, simple labels, and focused quality dimensions rather than a single all-purpose evaluator.
Validate judges against human-labeled examples, inspect disagreements, and hold out test data to avoid overfitting the rubric.
Use failure and regression datasets to test changes, then apply sampled production evaluations and feed new failures back into the development loop.
summary: Voss frames evaluations as testing for nondeterministic software and traces as execution logs composed of nested spans. A few plausible answers cannot establish reliability, especially when a prompt change can improve one behavior while breaking another. Agents add tool-selection errors, bad arguments, loops, and cascading misunderstandings, while rigid tests can also reject creatively valid solutions. The workshop instruments a two-turn Claude Agent SDK financial analyst with OpenInference and OpenTelemetry, sending research and report-writing activity to Arize AX. A parent span groups both turns so the whole task can be inspected together.

Before writing evaluators, Voss examines thirteen runs spanning varied companies, financial questions, and comparison requests. Some reports look polished but attempt unauthorized file writes and return references to unavailable reports; another execution searches repeatedly. He argues that domain experts should define success—correct company, recent evidence, useful recommendations, and a distinction between historical and forward-looking analysis. Open coding captures observed problems in ordinary language; axial coding subsequently groups them into root causes. Prioritization should consider both frequency and severity. Synthetic queries help initially, but production behavior should replace imagined cases as soon as it becomes available.

The first evaluator checks whether the requested stock ticker appears, catching an AWS-focused report that omits Amazon’s ticker. This inexpensive check is useful but cannot establish analytical quality. A built-in correctness judge then scores all thirteen reports incorrect because its knowledge does not cover their current financial claims. Giving the judge the agent’s research context instead produces seven unfaithful and six faithful reports: a more relevant signal about whether conclusions are supported, not proof that the sources themselves are true. A custom actionability judge adds explicit, observable pass/fail rules, bounded input sections, and examples. Voss recommends separate evaluators for separate dimensions, versioned rubrics, and a distinction between release-blocking guardrails and aspirational metrics.

Meta-evaluation compares judge predictions with human labels, using disagreements to expose ambiguous rules rather than assuming either side is always right. Voss discusses held-out data, precision and recall, and position, length, confidence, and self-preference biases. His displayed human labels are intentionally random, so the 46 percent agreement is instructional rather than a measured judge-quality result. Finally, failing traces become datasets, Claude proposes improved prompts from evaluation explanations and requirements, and experiments rerun tasks under the same evaluators. The polished demo reaches full actionability on its selected failure set, but Voss warns that real iteration is messier and live search remains variable. He recommends fixing data before prompts, considering model changes next, and leaving parameter tuning last. Production closes the loop through sampled evaluations, monitors, saved regressions, and verified fixes; coding agents should address recurring causes without gaming tests.
caveats: This is a vendor-led workshop using a small, deliberately flawed demonstration agent, not a production reliability study.
Voss explicitly says the displayed root-cause categories and human actionability labels were assigned randomly for demonstration.
The reported perfect actionability result concerns a selected demonstration failure set and does not establish general correctness, faithfulness, or production performance.
Sample-size recommendations and statements about human or judge performance are speaker guidance; supporting studies are not supplied in the transcript.
The publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently established. Watch and publisher duration is 6686 seconds, versus 6687 seconds in the videos-tab listing.
action_items: Read a dozen or more complete traces with a domain expert, write observable success criteria, and categorize failures before choosing metrics.
Start with one deterministic check, then add focused semantic judges with the evidence necessary to assess the task.
Build a human-labeled calibration set, inspect judge disagreements, and reserve held-out examples for testing rubric generalization.
Maintain both failing-case and passing-case datasets; compare prompt or model changes using the same evaluators and account for run-to-run variability.
Run sampled production evaluations and supply coding agents with requirements plus grouped failure explanations, verifying proposed fixes through experiments.

videos.title: From Raw Documents to AI-Ready Data — Leo Platzer & Jeff Koss
videos.overview: Jeff Koss and Leo Platzer demonstrate how document discovery, metadata enrichment, sensitivity screening, deduplication, and refresh workflows can turn a small RAG pilot into a maintained data product. Their central argument is that retrieval quality depends on curating the corpus before documents ever reach the model.
key_points: A successful pilot over forty curated documents does not resolve discovery, sensitivity, conflicting versions, or maintenance problems across tens of thousands of files.
Use-case-specific taxonomies can classify documents and conditionally extract more detailed metadata only from relevant categories.
Evidence views, human feedback, and sensitivity checks support review of automated tagging rather than requiring users to trust labels alone.
Data slices combine relevance, quality, freshness, and sensitivity criteria into a reusable, refreshable input for downstream systems.
Duplicated and stale documents can crowd retrieval results, making their impact on agent context larger than their share of the corpus.
Metadata-derived folder summaries and indexes can help coding agents locate relevant material without reading every file.
summary: Koss introduces an illustrative manufacturing company building a legal-operations chatbot over SharePoint documents. Its forty-file pilot can parse, chunk, embed, and retrieve information successfully, but expanding toward more than eighty thousand files creates a different problem: finding relevant agreements, excluding sensitive content, resolving duplicates and conflicting versions, and keeping information current. The scenario distinguishes the needs of engineering, knowledge management, legal operations, and enterprise transformation. A useful solution must satisfy all of them and become a repeatable process rather than a one-off document selection exercise.

The demonstration starts with 339 ingested files and builds a taxonomy—a tree of tags—using manual definitions, reusable tags, imported classification values, or AI suggestions. Conditional branches extract contract types only after a document has been identified as legal or contractual material. Users can filter the resulting metadata, inspect evidence behind a classification, and give feedback. Sensitivity detection combines AI-based classification with contextual pattern matching. Additional quality checks identify duplicates, conflicts, freshness constraints, and required metadata. These criteria define a data slice that can be delivered through an SDK, with scheduled updates intended to incorporate additions and deletions from SharePoint.

Platzer explains why corpus hygiene affects downstream retrieval disproportionately. Multiple versions or redundant chunks can occupy top-ranked retrieval slots, leaving little room for useful evidence. He reports an example in which a corpus with thirty percent stale or duplicate files can produce context containing up to eighty percent stale material. He also reports roughly doubled recall at one and a ten-to-fifteen-percent improvement in task completion in multi-hop RAG evaluations after curation. These are presenter-reported results without enough methodological detail to establish how broadly they transfer. The mechanism is nevertheless concrete: removing redundant or obsolete material changes what the retriever can place in the model’s limited context.

The final live example uses the SDK to generate a context repository from SharePoint metadata. Folder-level context files describe document types, topics, purpose, when to consult the folder, and example questions, while an index helps agents navigate the hierarchy. This lets Claude Code or Codex assess relevance without first opening every underlying document, with potential token savings. The speakers conclude by offering short proof-of-concept engagements that generate metadata, sensitivity and quality reports, and a use-case-specific taxonomy. Their broader recommendation is to treat document curation as maintained infrastructure supporting both RAG chatbots and agent context discovery.
caveats: North River Manufacturing is introduced as a demo scenario; its claimed reduction from months of preparation to days should not be treated as an independently documented customer outcome.
The retrieval and task-completion improvements lack dataset details, baselines, sample sizes, and a clear statement of whether percentage changes are relative or absolute.
Displayed model confidence scores are described by the presenters but are not shown to be calibrated probabilities of correctness.
The transcript uses inconsistent spellings for the product and SDK names; the summary does not infer an official spelling beyond the supplied wording.
The publisher transcript is untimed, and its semantic completeness is not independently established.
action_items: Audit a representative document collection for relevance, sensitive content, duplication, conflicting versions, and freshness before expanding a RAG pilot.
Define a use-case-specific taxonomy with conditional extraction rules and review classification evidence with domain experts.
Create a filtered data slice with explicit inclusion criteria and scheduled handling of source additions and deletions.
Compare retrieval and task outcomes before and after deduplication and freshness filtering on the same evaluation tasks.
Generate folder-level context summaries and a navigation index from reviewed metadata to reduce unnecessary document reads by agents.

videos.title: From Vibes to Production: Evaluating and Shipping AI Agents That Work 201 — Laurie Voss, Arize AI
videos.overview: Laurie Voss demonstrates an observability-to-repair workflow in which a coding agent inspects production traces, identifies behavioral problems, and modifies a toy-store shopping agent. He then presents Arize Signal as a continuous version of that workflow, while audience questions expose important limits around regression testing, compliance, and evaluating the repair agent itself.
key_points: Because agents can take different paths on identical inputs, Voss treats aggregated execution traces—not source code alone—as the evidence of actual behavior.
Traces expose tool calls, model calls, latency, cost, inputs, and outputs; semantic quality failures can occur even when requests return successful status codes.
The proposed improvement loop progresses from traces to evaluations, clustered failure signals, suggested fixes, and subsequent evaluation.
In the Wonder Toys demonstration, agent skills enable Claude Code to retrieve Arize traces and identify search problems, including missing price filtering.
Signal is described as periodically analyzing traces and offering GitHub issues, dataset additions, evaluator creation, or repository-connected pull requests.
Regression evaluations are the proposed safeguard against fixes breaking existing behavior; evaluator creation still requires user approval rather than happening automatically.
The session does not resolve the broader assurance problem for autonomous code changes in regulated settings, despite describing on-premises deployment and internal evaluation of Signal.
summary: Voss frames this advanced workshop as a response to two successive human bottlenecks. Reading individual traces becomes impractical at production volume; reading large numbers of evaluation results can then become another bottleneck. Since an agent may choose different tools and intermediate steps on repeated runs, he argues that traces across many executions are the operational source of truth. Evaluators compress those executions into scores and explanations, and another agent can group recurring failures into actionable patterns. His proposed next step is observability that not only reports behavior but feeds a coding agent enough evidence to improve it.

The hands-on example is Wonder Toys, a shopping application built with the OpenAI Agents SDK. Voss asks Claude Code to add Arize AX observability using existing credentials and repository-provided skills. He describes this as largely enabling and routing instrumentation rather than implementing tracing from scratch. Once traces appear, the agent retrieves them through the AX command line and inspects tool behavior. Importantly, there are no error spans to explain the poor experience: requests can return successfully while searches produce empty or meaningless results. The analysis reports excessive zero-result searches, all-null arguments, overly restrictive age filtering, and missing price-filter support.

Voss steers the coding agent toward adding price filtering, then demonstrates a successful request for toys under nine dollars and inspects the resulting trace. This establishes the basic workflow from instrumentation to diagnosis to modification, but the demonstration has qualifications: he initially runs the already-fixed application, and Claude subsequently copies the solution from a neighboring pre-solved directory. The session therefore illustrates the interaction pattern more convincingly than it establishes independent automated debugging. Signal extends the pattern by running inside AX, reportedly every six hours by default, finding issues such as invented age constraints and inappropriate responses to harmful or off-domain requests. Its outputs can become issues, evaluation examples, evaluator suggestions, or pull requests when the repository is connected.

The closing questions clarify boundaries around this automation. Voss recommends regression evaluations to detect losses in previously good behavior, and demonstrates asking the in-product Alyx assistant to create a safety evaluator. Signal does not automatically create its own evaluators because they consume time and money. He says Signal has its own internal evaluation suite, telemetry, and LLM judges assessing its outputs. At the time described, Arize pays its execution costs, and on-premises deployment is the compliance option rather than an on-device version. A question about trusting autonomous changes in finance and healthcare is largely deferred to another talk, leaving the assurance architecture substantially unexplained.
caveats: The supplied publisher transcript has no usable timestamps, and its semantic completeness is not independently proven.
The watch and publisher duration is 2536 seconds; the videos-tab duration is 2537 seconds.
The live repair is confounded by an initially selected pre-solved application and subsequent copying from an adjacent solved directory.
Signal capabilities, pricing, and deployment options are speaker descriptions at the time of the workshop, not independently verified product guarantees.
The regulated-industry question is deferred rather than substantively answered, and no production-scale reliability measurements are presented.
action_items: Instrument model calls, tool calls, and agent turns, then inspect latency, cost, and semantic outcomes rather than relying only on error statuses.
Give a trace-analysis agent explicit platform skills and ask it to cluster recurring behavioral failures before selecting a repair.
Turn discovered failures into evaluation examples and run regression evaluations before accepting generated fixes.
Separate suggested issues and pull requests from deployment approval, and require additional assurance work for regulated workflows.
Evaluate the diagnostic and repair agent itself using traceable outputs and a dedicated evaluation suite.

videos.title: Your LLM Judge Is a Confident Liar: Building Better Verifiers — Browserbase
videos.overview: Browserbase's Miguel and Microsoft's Corby explain why web-agent judges can substantially overstate success and present a rubric-and-evidence-based verifier designed to reduce that error. They connect verifier quality to human agreement, supervised-training data quality, and the limits of automated research without human guidance.
key_points: Dynamic websites, multiple valid solution paths, and environmental failures make deterministic web-agent evaluation difficult, but replacing it with a weak LLM judge can create misleading success metrics.
The speakers report that the same Fara-7B results scored approximately 74% success with the official WebVoyager judge and approximately 38% with their verifier.

Their verifier generates task-specific criteria, retrieves relevant screenshots for each criterion, checks claims against observed state, and returns both partial-credit process scores and a Boolean outcome.
Rubrics should avoid unrequested requirements and prevent one upstream mistake from automatically losing credit on every downstream step.
Process and outcome scores distinguish controllable agent mistakes from external obstacles, such as a requested product being out of stock.
Reported validation includes human-comparable agreement, held-out annotated trajectories, and improved models trained on fixed-size datasets filtered by the stronger verifier.
Unguided automated research reproduced only part of the human-designed verifier's agreement, while automation primed with human findings reportedly exceeded the team's earlier results.
summary: Miguel and Corby begin with the evaluation problem encountered while improving Stagehand and browser agents. Static, deterministically checked sites became expensive to maintain as tasks grew longer and capabilities improved. Real websites change, valid trajectories differ, and environmental blockages can prevent completion without proving that the agent behaved poorly. LLM judges offer flexibility, but the speakers found that existing benchmark verifiers could confidently approve failures. They illustrate the stakes with Fara-7B: the official WebVoyager judge reportedly assigned roughly 74% success, while their more human-aligned verifier assigned roughly 38%. An inaccurate reward or filtering signal can therefore optimize apparent competence rather than actual task completion.

Their universal verifier first converts a task into a rubric, then ranks trajectory screenshots by relevance to each criterion and evaluates the strongest evidence. It checks discrepancies between the agent's claims and the environment, producing a scored rubric and a separate success Boolean. Four design principles shape this process: assess only requested requirements, isolate errors across criteria, inspect screenshots rather than trusting narration, and distinguish controllable from uncontrollable failures. For example, a hotel-and-coffee-shop task should not acquire an extra requirement to report the hotel's total price. If an agent chooses the wrong band member when comparing surname lengths but correctly finds that person's net worth, the process rubric should recognize the successful downstream research without declaring the whole task successful.

Separating process from outcome also handles external obstacles. An agent that correctly finds an unavailable plush toy may deserve full process credit while still failing to achieve the purchase outcome. Evidence checking catches subtler failures too, such as reporting a paper's improvement as 6.2% when its abstract says 2.8%. To validate the verifier, the team collected expert judgments and reports a Cohen's kappa around 0.58, comparable to agreement between human annotators. They also report eliminating false positives in the evaluated sample. A complementary experiment held training-set size constant at 3,000 or 9,000 trajectories: supervised models trained on examples selected by the better verifier performed better than those using the baseline filter.

The final experiments examine whether automated research can build the verifier itself. The speakers' roughly thirty experiments took three weeks; an unguided automated loop ran comparable experimentation in about a day but reached only about 70% of their agreement level. Priming automation with their findings reportedly surpassed their earlier performance, suggesting a division of labor between human principles and automated search. In questions, they explain that about fifty labeled trajectories supported iteration while roughly one hundred were held out and independently double-annotated. They identify trained human verification as the gold standard, describe released code and CUAVerifierBench labels, and discuss extending the approach to desktop tasks with terminal and log evidence.
caveats: The supplied publisher transcript is untimed, and semantic completeness is not independently proven.

Reported success rates, false-positive reductions, training gains, and automated-research results are speaker claims; the supplied material does not include the paper's detailed tables or full experimental configuration.
The reported absence of false positives concerns an evaluated sample, not a guarantee of zero false positives in deployment.
The held-out evaluation is described as approximately one hundred trajectories; broader generalization to desktop tasks remains work in progress.

Human annotators saw verifier judgments after making initial judgments, so the transcript's description does not establish that every reported agreement measure was fully independent of verifier feedback.
action_items: Audit an existing agent judge against independently labeled trajectories before using its scores for model comparison, rewards, or training-data selection.
Generate task-specific rubrics that exclude unrequested requirements and score downstream work without mechanically cascading an earlier error.
Ground each criterion in relevant screenshots and compare the final answer with the actual observed environment.
Track process quality separately from task completion so environmental failures do not distort the signal about controllable agent behavior.
Reserve a held-out, double-annotated evaluation set and test verifier value through downstream training experiments, not agreement metrics alone.

videos.title: What Is an Inference Engine, Anyway? — Charles Frye, Modal
videos.overview: Charles Frye opens up the architecture behind systems such as SGLang and vLLM, showing how scheduling, GPU execution, and cache management turn a model into an efficient service. The workshop ties engine design to workload-specific latency and throughput goals, then explains major optimizations and the observability needed to diagnose correctness and performance failures.
key_points: Inference configuration should begin with workload characteristics: request rate, input and output lengths, prefix reuse, time to first token, and intertoken latency.
An inference server adds external I/O around an engine whose principal components include preprocessing, scheduling, model runners, and postprocessing.
The scheduler is a logically centralized gatekeeper to expensive GPU work; CPU-side delays can leave accelerators idle even when kernels are highly optimized.
Prefill processes many input tokens with higher arithmetic intensity, while sequential decoding repeatedly accesses model weights and often faces memory-bandwidth constraints.
KV caching and prefix sharing save recomputation but make memory capacity, cache layout, and request placement operationally important.
CUDA graphs reduce host launch overhead, and speculative decoding uses parallel verification of proposed tokens to accelerate otherwise sequential generation.
Production diagnosis requires deployment-level quality evaluations, token-ID logging, queue and latency metrics, and deeper CPU/GPU profiling when necessary.
summary: Frye distinguishes merely generating tokens from building an inference engine with favorable economics. He groups workloads into interactive chat and tool use, background agents, and data processors. These differ in output length, prefix reuse, and latency tolerance: interactive sessions need responsive token delivery, background work can tolerate longer waits, and document extraction often prioritizes aggregate throughput. He recommends measuring request rates, input and output token distributions, reusable prefixes, time to first token, and intertoken latency. Prefill and decode are effectively different sub-workloads: prefill performs substantial computation across an input sequence, while decode does much less arithmetic per request but repeats across generated tokens.

The architectural walkthrough follows a request from HTTP or RPC handling through tokenization, scheduling, model execution, detokenization, and response delivery. SGLang supplies the main process diagram, with differences from vLLM noted throughout. The scheduler constructs batches and manages scarce resources; model runners invoke GPU operations. Although GPU execution is the expensive component, a logically centralized scheduler can become its gatekeeper and bottleneck. Separate processes permit independent control flows and avoid Python's interpreter-lock constraints. Python remains useful because of its accelerator ecosystem and C/C++ interoperability, while Frye identifies the host-side scheduler as a plausible future target for a compiled-language rewrite rather than advocating a wholesale rewrite.

Performance comes from coordinating shared kernel libraries, model-specific forward-pass implementations, and engine-specific batching decisions. Attention and matrix multiplication backends often overlap across engines, so differentiation frequently lies in keeping the GPU supplied with work. KV caching avoids recomputing prior attention state, and exact shared prefixes allow reuse across requests. The engine must manage cache capacity and layout; cache thrashing or spilling is described as a sign of an overloaded deployment. CUDA graph capture replaces many individual host-side launches with a captured operation graph. Speculative decoding has a smaller model propose tokens and the target verify them in parallel, turning parts of decode into small prefills. Correct rejection sampling preserves the target distribution subject to numerical details; actual speedups depend on speculation quality and workload.

The final section separates application behavior problems, engine-induced model-quality bugs, and performance regressions. Frye recommends evaluating the actual deployed endpoint, retaining traces that connect user feedback to requests, and logging token IDs to investigate tokenizer or chat-template mistakes. Broad performance telemetry helps reveal long-running degradation and differences across replicas. In his art-installation example, a traffic spike increases queueing, time to first token, and intertoken latency; additional replicas relieve congestion.
